core: Working definition: vitamins are organic compounds the body needs in small amounts to grow, develop, and work properly (attributed to MedlinePlus/OpenStax)
The 13 vitamins the body needs; each has specific jobs; all are essential
Why the body needs them: coenzymes (B vitamins release energy from carbs/fats/protein), vision (vitamin A), immunity (A, C), bone health (D, K)
Fat-soluble vs water-soluble: stored in fat vs not stored, with the consequence that daily intake matters differently
Essential idea: the body cannot make most vitamins (only D via sunlight and some K); food must supply them
Getting them from food: a balanced diet with variety is the best way; you can usually get all vitamins from food
Deficiency and excess both matter: too little causes health problems; high doses of some vitamins can cause problems
Honest framing: vitamins are helpers (sparks), not fuel; they enable energy release but supply no fuel themselves
supporting: B12 as the exception among water-soluble vitamins (stored in the liver for years)
Fat-soluble vitamins absorbed more easily in the presence of dietary fat
Original worked example tracing fat- and water-soluble vitamins through one dinner
Vitamin C deficiency linked to anemia; vitamin A deficiency linked to night blindness (illustrative examples only)

claims.claim: Vitamins are organic compounds (substances) the body needs in small amounts to grow, develop, and function properly; MedlinePlus describes them as substances the body needs to grow and develop normally, and OpenStax describes them as nutrients the body needs in small amounts to function and stay healthy.
There are 13 vitamins the body needs (A, C, D, E, K, and the eight B vitamins), each with specific jobs, and none can substitute for another.

Vitamins are essential: the body cannot make most of them and must get them from food; the body can make vitamin D with sunlight and some vitamin K (Harvard: micronutrients 'are not produced in our bodies and must be derived from the food we eat').

Vitamins divide into two classes: fat-soluble (A, D, E, K), which dissolve in fat, are absorbed with dietary fat, and are stored in the liver and fatty tissue; and water-soluble (vitamin C and the B vitamins), which are not stored and leave the body through urine in excess, so a regular supply matters (exception: B12 is stored in the liver).

Many vitamins work as coenzymes, helper molecules that partner with enzymes; notably the B vitamins assist the enzymes that metabolize carbohydrates, fats, and proteins, releasing energy for body cells.

Specific vitamin jobs: vitamin A helps form and maintain the retina and supports vision and immunity; vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium for bone health; vitamin C supports wound healing; vitamin K is required for normal blood clotting and participates in bone metabolism.
Vitamin deficiency, getting too little of a vitamin, can cause health problems; examples: not enough vitamin C can cause anemia, and vitamin A prevents night blindness (MedlinePlus).
Because fat-soluble vitamins are stored, daily intake is not required, but excess intake of fat-soluble vitamins can accumulate and cause toxicity; high doses of some vitamins can cause problems.
The best way to get enough vitamins is a balanced diet with a variety of foods, and you can usually get all your vitamins from the foods you eat.

Vitamins enable the body to use fuel rather than serving as fuel themselves: they act as helpers in the reactions that release energy from carbohydrates, fats, and proteins, and taking vitamins without the food substrates provides nothing for coenzyme action.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether vitamins provide energy or only help the body use it
positions: Popular product claims frame vitamins as energy boosters, implying more vitamins means more energy
Authoritative sources describe vitamins as coenzymes/helpers in energy metabolism; they supply no calories or fuel themselves
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Sources agree vitamins assist the reactions that release energy from macronutrients and provide no fuel of their own. The lesson teaches the helper framing and does not repeat energy claims.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether most people need vitamin supplements
positions: Supplement marketing suggests widespread need for extra vitamins
Authoritative guidance: a balanced, varied diet is the best way to get enough vitamins, and high doses of some vitamins can cause problems
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the food-first guidance factually and gives no supplementation advice; the supplements sibling topic owns that discussion.

unsupportedExistingClaims: Generated draft claimed 'Vitamins is a foundational concept in Nutrition' and 'College courses use vitamins as a building block' — generic boilerplate with no factual content; replaced entirely.
Generated draft gave no definition, no 13-vitamin list, no fat/water-soluble distinction, and no health facts; all lesson content was written fresh from verified sources.

sourceRecords.title: Vitamins (Medical Encyclopedia)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Provides the 13 essential vitamins list, the definition that vitamins are needed for normal cell function, growth, and development, the fat-soluble (A, D, E, K; stored in liver, fatty tissue, muscles; absorbed more easily with dietary fat) vs water-soluble (C and B vitamins; not stored; excess leaves via urine; regular intake needed; B12 exception) classification, per-vitamin jobs (A: retina/vision; D: calcium absorption and bone health; C: wound healing and iron absorption; K: normal blood clotting; B vitamins: metabolism), and the deficiency framing.

sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: vitamins are substances the body needs to grow and develop normally; 13 vitamins; you can usually get all your vitamins from the foods you eat; the body can also make vitamins D and K; each vitamin has specific jobs; low levels cause health problems (vitamin C deficiency can cause anemia; vitamin A prevents night blindness); the best way to get enough vitamins is a balanced diet with a variety of foods; high doses of some vitamins can cause problems.

sourceRecords.title: Nutrition for Nurses (2e), Section 3.1: Vitamins
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Internet Archive capture of 2024-04-17 (web.archive.org/web/20240417150516) because openstax.org blocks direct fetching. Supports: vitamins as nutrients the body needs in small amounts to function and stay healthy; the two classes (fat-soluble A, D, E, K absorbed with fats, stored in fatty tissue and liver, with roles in vision, bone health, immune function, and coagulation; water-soluble dissolved in water, excess excreted in urine); B vitamins as coenzymes assisting metabolism of carbohydrates, fat, and protein; fat-soluble toxicity from stored excess; obtaining vitamins through foods is preferred and a supplement without the food substrate provides nothing for coenzyme action; vitamin D synthesized by the body from a cholesterol precursor with UV light.

sourceRecords.title: The Nutrition Source: Vitamins and Minerals
sourceRecords.provider: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: vitamins and minerals are micronutrients required by the body for normal functions; these micronutrients are not produced in the body and must come from food; vitamins are organic substances classified as fat-soluble or water-soluble; fat-soluble vitamins dissolve in fat and tend to accumulate; water-soluble vitamins cannot be stored and unused amounts are lost primarily through urine.
